nodes.title: Engineering Foundations
nodes.essence: Every computation is a physical event.

nodes.title: Physics of Computation
nodes.essence: A computer is a physical system, and everything it does is something physics allows. This area answers the question: what physical facts must be true for a machine to store and transform information, and what limits do those facts impose? Three bodies of physics carry the load.

nodes.title: Electromagnetism and Charge
nodes.essence: Every bit in a conventional computer is a physical arrangement of electric charge or magnetic orientation, and every operation moves charge from one place to another.

nodes.title: Quantum Mechanics and Band Theory
nodes.essence: Classical physics cannot explain why copper conducts, glass insulates and silicon sits usefully in between.

nodes.title: Thermodynamics and Energy
nodes.essence: Computation is a physical process, so it consumes energy and produces heat, and the heat must be removed. Thermodynamics tells us three things that shape every computer.

nodes.title: Electrical Circuits
nodes.essence: Electromagnetism is too detailed to design with directly.

nodes.title: Circuit Laws
nodes.essence: Circuit theory is the first great abstraction in the stack.

nodes.title: Capacitance and Timing
nodes.essence: A digital signal cannot change instantly, because every wire and every transistor gate is a capacitor that must be filled or drained through some resistance.

nodes.title: Noise and Signal Integrity
nodes.essence: Real voltages are never exactly what the designer intended. Thermal agitation, neighbouring wires, supply fluctuations, reflections on long wires and even cosmic rays all add unwanted signal, called noise.

nodes.title: Semiconductor Devices
nodes.essence: Computing needs a switch: a device in which one signal controls whether another flows, that can be made tiny, cheap and in astronomical numbers, and whose output can drive further switches.

nodes.title: Doping and the PN Junction
nodes.essence: Pure silicon conducts poorly, but adding a tiny, precisely controlled amount of the right impurity, a process called doping, raises its conductivity by many orders of magnitude and decides whether the current is carried mainly by electrons (n-type) or holes (p-type).

nodes.title: The MOSFET
nodes.essence: The Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor (MOSFET) is a voltage-controlled switch, and it is the most manufactured device in history. A gate electrode sits on a thin insulator above a channel of silicon between two doped terminals, the source and the drain.

nodes.title: CMOS
nodes.essence: Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) is the circuit style used by almost every digital chip made since the late 1980s.

nodes.title: Fabrication and Scaling
nodes.essence: Integrated circuits are made by printing patterns onto a silicon wafer, layer by layer, using light projected through masks, then etching, doping and depositing material where the pattern allows.

nodes.title: Signals and Systems
nodes.essence: Circuits tell you what voltages and currents do; signals and systems tell you what they mean and how they behave over time. A signal is a quantity that carries information; a system transforms signals.

nodes.title: Analog vs Digital
nodes.essence: The physical world is analog: voltages, positions and sound pressures take continuous values and change continuously in time. A digital system deliberately ignores most of that continuum.

nodes.title: Sampling and Quantization
nodes.essence: To compute on a real-world signal, a system must turn a continuous function of time into a finite list of numbers. Sampling discretises time: it records the signal's value at regular instants. Quantisation discretises value: it rounds each sample to one of a finite set of levels.

nodes.title: Feedback and Control
nodes.essence: Feedback means measuring a system's output and using it to adjust the input. Negative feedback opposes deviations: it makes a system precise and robust even when its parts are imprecise, at the cost of raw gain and with a risk of oscillation if the loop reacts too late.

nodes.title: Engineering Method
nodes.essence: The other four areas of this layer describe what physical computing is made of. This one describes how engineers think when they build with it.

nodes.title: Tradeoffs and Constraints
nodes.essence: Engineering is the art of choosing well when you cannot have everything. Every design lives inside constraints, some set by physics (the speed of light, heat removal, noise), some by economics (cost, schedule, volume) and some by people (skills, maintainability, regulations).

nodes.title: Reliability and Redundancy
nodes.essence: Every component eventually fails, and a system built from many components fails more often than any one of them.

nodes.title: Measurement and Modeling
nodes.essence: Engineers do not reason about reality directly; they reason about models of it, and they check those models by measurement. A model is a deliberate simplification: an ideal switch for a transistor, a lumped resistor for a wire, a queue for a server.

nodes.title: Mathematical Foundations
nodes.essence: This layer is the formal root of Computer Science (CS).

nodes.title: Logic
nodes.essence: Logic answers the question "when does a conclusion follow from premises?" and answers it precisely enough that a machine can check the answer.

nodes.title: Propositional Logic
nodes.essence: Propositional logic is the study of statements that are either true or false, combined with connectives such as AND, OR, NOT and IMPLIES.

nodes.title: Predicate Logic
nodes.essence: Predicate logic (first-order logic) extends propositional logic with objects, predicates that hold of objects, functions on objects, and the quantifiers "for all" (∀) and "there exists" (∃).

nodes.title: Proof Techniques
nodes.essence: A proof is a finite argument that a claim follows from agreed premises, where each step is justified by a rule of logic.

nodes.title: Sets, Relations and Functions
nodes.essence: This area supplies the raw material from which almost every other mathematical object in computer science is built. A set is a collection; a relation is a set of pairs; a function is a relation with one output per input.

nodes.title: Sets
nodes.essence: A set is a collection of distinct objects with no order and no repetition, determined entirely by which things are members.

nodes.title: Relations and Orders
nodes.essence: A binary relation on a set A is a set of ordered pairs from A × A: it records which elements are related to which. Relations are how mathematics talks about connections: "is less than", "calls", "happens before", "depends on", "is reachable from".

nodes.title: Functions and Cardinality
nodes.essence: A function f: A → B is a relation that pairs every element of its domain A with exactly one element of its codomain B. Functions are the mathematical model of a deterministic computation: same input, same output.

nodes.title: Discrete Mathematics
nodes.essence: Discrete mathematics studies structures made of separate, countable pieces: finite sets, integers, graphs, sequences defined step by step.

nodes.title: Combinatorics
nodes.essence: Combinatorics is the mathematics of counting finite structures: how many ways to arrange, choose or distribute things under constraints.

nodes.title: Graph Theory
nodes.essence: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges; it is the mathematical form of "things and the connections between them".

nodes.title: Induction and Recurrences
nodes.essence: Induction and recursion are the same idea seen from two sides. Recursion defines something for all sizes by saying what to do at the smallest size and how to build size n from smaller sizes; induction proves something for all sizes by the same two steps.

nodes.title: Number Theory
nodes.essence: Number theory studies the integers: divisibility, primes, remainders and the arithmetic of "clock" systems where numbers wrap around. For a computer scientist it matters for three reasons. Machine integers are modular arithmetic: a 32-bit register computes modulo 2^32.

nodes.title: Algebra
nodes.essence: Algebra is the study of operations and the laws they obey. Instead of asking what a particular number equals, it asks what follows from rules such as "this operation is associative" or "every element has an inverse".

nodes.title: Boolean Algebra
nodes.essence: Boolean algebra is the algebra of two values, 0 and 1, under the operations AND (·), OR (+) and NOT (complement). It turns logical reasoning into symbol manipulation with equational laws, much as ordinary algebra does for numbers.

nodes.title: Abstract Algebra
nodes.essence: Abstract algebra studies operations by their laws rather than by what they operate on. A group, ring or field is any set with operations that obey a stated list of axioms, and every theorem proved from those axioms holds for every example at once.

nodes.title: Linear Algebra
nodes.essence: Linear algebra studies vectors, and the functions between vector spaces that preserve addition and scaling: linear maps, represented by matrices.

nodes.title: Continuous Mathematics
nodes.essence: Continuous mathematics deals with quantities that vary smoothly: real numbers, rates of change, areas, and functions that can be approximated locally by straight lines. A computer is a discrete machine, so it may seem odd to need it.

nodes.title: Calculus
nodes.essence: Calculus is the mathematics of change and accumulation. The derivative measures how fast a quantity changes, by approximating a function near a point with a straight line (or, in many dimensions, with a linear map).

nodes.title: Optimization
nodes.essence: Optimization is the problem of choosing the input that minimises (or maximises) an objective function, possibly subject to constraints.

nodes.title: Fourier Analysis
nodes.essence: Fourier analysis writes a signal (a sound wave, an image row, a list of numbers) as a sum of sinusoids, each with its own frequency, amplitude and phase. It is a change of basis: the same information in coordinates where many operations become simple.

nodes.title: Probability and Statistics
nodes.essence: Probability and statistics are the mathematics of reasoning under uncertainty. Probability starts from a model of chance and predicts what data will look like; statistics starts from data and infers what the model must be. Computer science needs both directions.

nodes.title: Probability
nodes.essence: Probability is the mathematics of uncertainty: it assigns numbers between 0 and 1 to events in a way that is consistent, so that degrees of belief or long-run frequencies can be combined by rules.

nodes.title: Random Variables and Distributions
nodes.essence: A random variable is a function that assigns a number to each outcome of a random experiment: the latency of a request, the number of collisions in a hash table, the bit error count in a frame.

nodes.title: Statistical Inference
nodes.essence: Statistical inference runs probability backwards. Probability asks "given the model, how likely is this data?"; inference asks "given this data, what can we say about the model?".

nodes.title: Markov Chains
nodes.essence: A Markov chain is a random process whose next state depends only on its current state, not on how it got there.

nodes.title: Theory of Computation
nodes.essence: Theory of computation asks what information is, what machines can do with it, and at what cost, before any machine is built.

nodes.title: Information Theory
nodes.essence: Information theory asks how much there is to say and how reliably it can be said.

nodes.title: Entropy and Information
nodes.essence: Information theory measures how much uncertainty a message removes, independent of what the message means.

nodes.title: Source Coding and Compression
nodes.essence: Source coding is the problem of representing the output of a source in as few bits as possible. Shannon's source coding theorem answers it exactly: a source with entropy H bits per symbol can be losslessly compressed to any rate above H bits per symbol and to no rate below it.

nodes.title: Channel Capacity and Error Correction
nodes.essence: Every physical channel (wire, radio link, flash cell) corrupts some of what passes through it.

nodes.title: Kolmogorov Complexity
nodes.essence: Kolmogorov complexity measures the information in a single object, with no probability model: K(x) is the length of the shortest program that prints the string x and halts.

nodes.title: Automata and Formal Languages
nodes.essence: This area asks: what can a machine with a given kind of memory recognise? It turns every computational problem into a question about a language, a set of strings (the inputs whose answer is "yes"), and then studies which machines can decide membership.

nodes.title: Finite Automata and Regular Languages
nodes.essence: A finite automaton is the simplest model of a computer: a machine with a fixed, finite amount of memory that reads its input once, left to right, and then says yes or no.

nodes.title: Context-Free Grammars and Pushdown Automata
nodes.essence: Context-free grammars describe nested structure: balanced parentheses, expressions, blocks inside blocks. A grammar is a set of rewrite rules such as E → E + T | T, each replacing a single symbol regardless of its surroundings (hence "context-free").

nodes.title: The Chomsky Hierarchy
nodes.essence: The Chomsky hierarchy ranks grammars by how much freedom their rules have and pairs each rank with a class of machines by how much memory those machines have.

nodes.title: Computability
nodes.essence: Computability asks the most basic question in Computer Science (CS): what can be computed at all, given unlimited time and memory? Its answer has two halves.

nodes.title: Turing Machines
nodes.essence: A Turing Machine (TM) is a finite automaton given an unbounded tape it can read, write and move along in both directions.

nodes.title: Lambda Calculus
nodes.essence: The lambda calculus, introduced by Alonzo Church in the early 1930s, is a model of computation with only three constructs: variables, function definition and function application.

nodes.title: The Church–Turing Thesis
nodes.essence: The Church–Turing thesis says that every function that can be computed by an effective procedure (a finite, mechanical, step-by-step method that a careful clerk could follow without insight) can be computed by a Turing machine.

nodes.title: The Halting Problem and Undecidability
nodes.essence: Some precisely stated questions about programs have no algorithm that always answers them correctly. The first and most important is the halting problem: given a program and an input, will the program eventually stop?

nodes.title: Complexity
nodes.essence: Computability separates what can be computed from what cannot. Complexity asks the next question: among computable problems, what does each one fundamentally cost? Cost means time, memory, random bits, parallel depth or quantum operations, measured as a function of input size.

nodes.title: Asymptotic Analysis
nodes.essence: Asymptotic analysis describes how the resources an algorithm uses (time, memory, messages) grow as the input gets large, ignoring constant factors and small inputs. It does this with Big-O and its relatives, which compare functions by their eventual growth rate.

nodes.title: P, NP and NP-Completeness
nodes.essence: P is the class of decision problems that can be solved in polynomial time; NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) is the class whose "yes" answers can be checked in polynomial time given a short certificate.

nodes.title: Complexity Classes
nodes.essence: A complexity class is the set of problems solvable within a given budget of a given resource on a given kind of machine: polynomial time on a deterministic machine (P), polynomial space (PSPACE), polynomial time with random bits (BPP), polynomial time on a quantum computer (BQP), and so on.

nodes.title: Quantum Computation
nodes.essence: Classical complexity theory assumes the machine obeys classical physics: bits are definite and probabilities add. Quantum computation asks what changes if the machine instead obeys quantum mechanics, where the state is a vector of complex amplitudes that can interfere.

nodes.title: Qubits and Quantum Circuits
nodes.essence: A quantum computer stores information in qubits, whose state is a unit vector in a complex vector space rather than a definite 0 or 1.

nodes.title: Quantum Algorithms
nodes.essence: A handful of quantum algorithms show both how much faster quantum computers can be and how narrow that advantage is.

nodes.title: Digital Logic
nodes.essence: Digital logic is where computer science's two roots join. From the formal side comes Boolean algebra, a mathematical system of values 0 and 1 with operations AND, OR and NOT.

nodes.title: Number Representation
nodes.essence: Hardware stores and moves only fixed-width strings of bits. Programs need integers, real numbers and text. This area answers: how do we encode mathematical and human objects as finite bit patterns, and what do those encodings make cheap, expensive or impossible?

nodes.title: Binary and Positional Notation
nodes.essence: Digital hardware can reliably distinguish only two voltage levels, so everything a computer stores is a string of binary digits (bits).

nodes.title: Integers and Two's Complement
nodes.essence: Hardware integers are not mathematical integers. They are fixed-width bit patterns, and arithmetic on them wraps around modulo 2ⁿ.

nodes.title: Floating Point
nodes.essence: Floating point represents real numbers in a fixed number of bits as a sign, a significand and an exponent, the binary form of scientific notation.

nodes.title: Character Encoding
nodes.essence: Text is stored by mapping characters to numbers and numbers to bytes. That takes two separate decisions: a character set that assigns each abstract character a number (a code point), and an encoding that turns code points into byte sequences.

nodes.title: Combinational Logic
nodes.essence: Combinational logic is hardware that computes a function: its outputs depend only on its present inputs, with no memory of the past.

nodes.title: Logic Gates
nodes.essence: A logic gate is a physical circuit that computes a Boolean function of its inputs and drives its output to a clean, restored logic level after a short delay.

nodes.title: Logic Minimization
nodes.essence: Any Boolean function can be built directly from its truth table, but the direct circuit is usually far larger and slower than necessary. Logic minimisation finds an equivalent circuit that costs less: fewer gates, fewer literals, less depth, less power.

nodes.title: Arithmetic and Building Blocks
nodes.essence: Processors are not designed gate by gate. They are assembled from a small set of standard combinational blocks: multiplexers that select, decoders that route, adders that compute, comparators and shifters, and the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU) that combines them.

nodes.title: Sequential Logic
nodes.essence: Combinational logic computes functions; it cannot remember anything or do things in sequence. Sequential logic adds state, so that a circuit's output can depend on its history and a computation can proceed step by step.

nodes.title: Latches and Flip-Flops
nodes.essence: Combinational logic forgets: its output depends only on its present input. To compute over time, hardware must remember, and memory comes from feedback. Two inverters connected in a loop have two stable states and hold either one indefinitely while powered.

nodes.title: Clocking and Synchronous Design
nodes.essence: Synchronous design is the discipline that makes complex digital systems possible. All state lives in flip-flops driven by one shared clock; between flip-flops sits only combinational logic.

nodes.title: Finite State Machines
nodes.essence: A finite state machine (FSM) is the hardware realisation of a finite automaton: a register holding the current state, combinational logic that computes the next state from the current state and inputs, and logic that computes outputs.

nodes.title: Memory Cells
nodes.essence: A flip-flop costs about twenty transistors, far too many for billions of bits. Bulk memory uses much smaller cells in a grid of word lines (rows) and bit lines (columns), each storing the bit in a different physical form.

nodes.title: Hardware Design
nodes.essence: The previous three areas explain what digital circuits are made of. This one explains how real chips with billions of transistors are actually designed, built and signed off.

nodes.title: Hardware Description Languages
nodes.essence: Modern chips contain billions of transistors, far too many to draw.

nodes.title: FPGA and ASIC
nodes.essence: A digital design described in a Hardware Description Language (HDL) can become physical hardware in two main ways.

nodes.title: Timing and Power
nodes.essence: A digital design is correct only if it is fast enough and cool enough. Timing analysis checks that every signal path settles within the clock period, under every combination of manufacturing variation, voltage and temperature the chip may meet.

nodes.title: Computer Architecture
nodes.essence: Computer architecture answers one question: how do you turn a pile of gates and flip-flops into a machine that runs any program fast, and keep running the same programs as the hardware underneath changes every two years? The answer is a contract.

nodes.title: Instruction Set Architecture
nodes.essence: The Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is the boundary between hardware and software: the complete list of what a program can observe about a processor.

nodes.title: The ISA Contract
nodes.essence: An Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) is a specification of a processor as software sees it: a set of architectural state (registers, program counter, memory, control registers) and a set of instructions, each defined as a function from one state to the next.

nodes.title: RISC vs CISC
nodes.essence: Reduced Instruction Set Computer (RISC) and Complex Instruction Set Computer (CISC) are two philosophies for what to put in an Instruction Set Architecture (ISA).

nodes.title: Instruction Encoding and Addressing
nodes.essence: Every instruction must be written as a string of bits that a decoder can turn into control signals, and every operand must be named: a register number, a constant embedded in the instruction (an immediate), or a memory address computed from registers and constants.

nodes.title: Processor Microarchitecture
nodes.essence: Microarchitecture is how a processor core implements the Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) contract in gates and flip-flops.

nodes.title: Datapath and Control
nodes.essence: A processor core divides into two parts. The datapath holds and transforms data: the register file, the Arithmetic Logic Unit (ALU), adders for addresses, memory interfaces and the multiplexers and wires between them.

nodes.title: Pipelining
nodes.essence: Pipelining splits the execution of each instruction into stages and runs different instructions in different stages at the same time, like an assembly line.

nodes.title: Hazards and Branch Prediction
nodes.essence: A hazard is any situation in which the next instruction in a pipeline cannot proceed in the next cycle without risking a wrong result.

nodes.title: Superscalar and Out-of-Order Execution
nodes.essence: A superscalar core fetches, decodes and executes several instructions per cycle. An out-of-order core goes further: it executes each instruction as soon as its operands are ready, not when its turn comes in program order.

nodes.title: Memory Hierarchy
nodes.essence: Programs want memory that is large, fast and cheap. Physics allows any two.

nodes.title: Locality and Caching
nodes.essence: Real programs do not touch memory at random. They reuse data they touched recently (temporal locality) and touch addresses near ones they touched recently (spatial locality).

nodes.title: Cache Design
nodes.essence: A hardware cache is a fixed-size table of recently used memory lines, searched by address in a few cycles.

nodes.title: Virtual Memory Hardware
nodes.essence: Virtual memory gives every program its own private address space by inserting a translation between the addresses a program uses (virtual) and the locations in physical memory.

nodes.title: DRAM and Storage Devices
nodes.essence: Below the caches sit the memories that hold most of the data: Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM) for working memory, and non-volatile storage (NAND flash in Solid-State Drives (SSDs), and magnetic Hard Disk Drives (HDDs)) for everything that must survive power loss.

nodes.title: Parallel Architecture
nodes.essence: Around 2005, single-core performance growth slowed sharply. Clock frequency stopped rising because power density could no longer be cooled, and Instruction-Level Parallelism (ILP) inside one instruction stream had largely been harvested.

nodes.title: Multicore and Cache Coherence
nodes.essence: A multicore processor puts several complete cores on one chip, each with private level-1 (L1) and usually level-2 (L2) caches, sharing a last-level cache and main memory.

nodes.title: Memory Consistency Models
nodes.essence: A memory consistency model is the part of the Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) that says which values a load may return when several cores read and write shared memory.

nodes.title: SIMD and GPUs
nodes.essence: Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) execution applies one instruction to many data elements at once: one fetch, decode and scheduling decision drives 4, 8, 16 or more arithmetic lanes.

nodes.title: Domain-Specific Accelerators
nodes.essence: A domain-specific accelerator is hardware designed for one class of computation, such as neural-network inference, video encoding or encryption, rather than for arbitrary programs.

nodes.title: I/O and Interconnect
nodes.essence: A processor that cannot talk to the outside world is useless.

nodes.title: Buses and Interrupts
nodes.essence: A bus or interconnect is the shared or point-to-point communication path that links processors, memory and devices; an interrupt is a signal by which a device asks the processor to stop what it is doing and handle an event.

nodes.title: DMA and Devices
nodes.essence: Direct Memory Access (DMA) lets a device read and write main memory itself, without the processor copying each word.

nodes.title: Performance
nodes.essence: Computer architecture is a quantitative discipline: every feature is justified by how much faster, cheaper or more efficient it makes real programs, and every feature costs area, power and design effort. This area gathers the laws that make those judgements possible.

nodes.title: The Performance Equation
nodes.essence: The only honest measure of a computer's speed is the time it takes to run the programs you care about.

nodes.title: Amdahl's Law
nodes.essence: Amdahl's law says that the overall speedup from improving part of a system is limited by the fraction of time the improved part was used. If a fraction f of the run time is sped up by a factor s, the overall speedup is 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s).

nodes.title: Power and the End of Scaling
nodes.essence: For about thirty years, each new chip generation gave more transistors, faster transistors and the same power per unit area, all at once.

nodes.title: Algorithms and Data Structures
nodes.essence: An algorithm is a finite, precisely specified procedure that turns any valid input into the correct output. A data structure is a way of laying out information in memory so that the operations an algorithm needs are cheap.

nodes.title: Foundations
nodes.essence: Before you can say an algorithm is "good" you need two things: a proof that it is right and a way to count what it costs. This area supplies both.

nodes.title: Models of Computation
nodes.essence: To say an algorithm "takes O(n log n) time" you must first say what one unit of time is. A model of computation fixes this: which operations cost one step, how big a memory word is, and what is free.

nodes.title: Correctness and Invariants
nodes.essence: An algorithm is correct if, for every input satisfying its precondition, it halts and produces an output satisfying its postcondition. Testing samples a few inputs; proof covers all of them.

nodes.title: Amortized Analysis
nodes.essence: Some data structures do a little work most of the time and a lot of work occasionally. A dynamic array appends in O(1) until it fills, then copies everything. Worst-case analysis per operation would call append O(n), which badly overstates the cost of a long sequence.

nodes.title: Fundamental Data Structures
nodes.essence: A data structure is a representation of a collection plus a set of operations, chosen so that the operations a program needs most are cheap.

nodes.title: Arrays and Linked Lists
nodes.essence: There are only two ways to organise a sequence in memory. An array puts elements in consecutive addresses, so the address of element i is base + i × size, computed in one step.

nodes.title: Stacks and Queues
nodes.essence: A stack and a queue are collections that restrict which element you may remove. A stack returns the most recently added element (Last In, First Out, LIFO). A queue returns the least recently added (First In, First Out, FIFO).

nodes.title: Hash Tables
nodes.essence: A hash table stores key–value pairs so that lookup, insert and delete by exact key take O(1) expected time. It works by computing a hash function h(key) that maps any key to an index in an array of m slots, then storing the pair at (or near) that index.

nodes.title: Search Trees
nodes.essence: A binary search tree (BST) stores keys in nodes so that, at every node, all keys in the left subtree are smaller and all keys in the right subtree are larger. Searching follows one root-to-leaf path, comparing at each node, so it costs O(height).

nodes.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
nodes.essence: A priority queue holds items with priorities and supports insert and extract-min (or extract-max): always remove the most urgent item.

nodes.title: Union–Find
nodes.essence: A union–find (disjoint-set) structure maintains a partition of n elements into disjoint sets under two operations: find(x) returns a canonical representative of x's set, and union(x, y) merges two sets. It answers "are x and y in the same group?" while groups keep merging.

nodes.title: Design Paradigms
nodes.essence: Most algorithms are not invented from nothing. They are instances of a handful of strategies, each of which exploits a particular structure in the problem. This area answers: what structure does my problem have, and which strategy turns that structure into an efficient algorithm?

nodes.title: Divide and Conquer
nodes.essence: Divide and conquer solves a problem by splitting it into smaller independent instances of the same problem, solving each recursively, and combining their answers.

nodes.title: Greedy Algorithms
nodes.essence: A greedy algorithm builds a solution one piece at a time, always taking the choice that looks best right now, and never going back. That is fast (often just a sort or a priority queue plus a linear scan) but usually wrong.

nodes.title: Dynamic Programming
nodes.essence: Dynamic programming (DP) solves a problem by expressing its answer as a recurrence over smaller subproblems, then computing each distinct subproblem exactly once and storing the result.

nodes.title: Backtracking and Branch and Bound
nodes.essence: Many important problems (scheduling, satisfiability, puzzles, routing with constraints) have no known structure that greedy, divide and conquer or dynamic programming can exploit, and are NP-hard, so no polynomial algorithm is expected.

nodes.title: Randomized Algorithms
nodes.essence: A randomized algorithm flips coins as it runs. Its behaviour on a fixed input becomes a random variable, and we analyse expected running time or the probability of error over the algorithm's own random choices, not over a distribution of inputs.

nodes.title: Sorting and Searching
nodes.essence: Sorting puts n items in order; searching finds an item or a rank in a collection. They are the most studied problems in algorithms because nearly everything else uses them: sorted data makes search logarithmic, duplicates adjacent, merges linear and ranges contiguous.

nodes.title: Comparison Sorting
nodes.essence: A comparison sort orders n items using only a "less than" test between pairs, so it works for any type with a total order: numbers, strings, dates, tuples.

nodes.title: Non-Comparison Sorting
nodes.essence: Comparison sorts cannot do better than Ω(n log n) because each comparison yields one bit. If keys are integers, strings or anything with a fixed-width digit representation, you can learn far more per step by using a key's digits as an array index.

nodes.title: Searching and Selection
nodes.essence: Searching asks "where is key x?" and selection asks "which item has rank k?" (the minimum, the median, the 99th percentile).

nodes.title: Graph Algorithms
nodes.essence: A graph is a set of vertices joined by edges. It is the most general model of relationships: road networks, the Internet, social networks, call graphs, dependency graphs, state spaces, circuits. A huge range of practical questions reduce to a few graph problems: what can I reach?

nodes.title: Graph Traversal
nodes.essence: Graph traversal visits every vertex reachable from a starting point, each exactly once, in O(V + E) time for a graph with V vertices and E edges stored as adjacency lists.

nodes.title: Shortest Paths
nodes.essence: Given a graph with weighted edges, find the cheapest path from a source to every other vertex (single-source) or between every pair (all-pairs).

nodes.title: Minimum Spanning Trees
nodes.essence: Given a connected undirected graph with edge weights, a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) is a set of V − 1 edges that connects all V vertices with the smallest possible total weight.

nodes.title: Network Flow
nodes.essence: A flow network is a directed graph where each edge has a capacity, with a source s and a sink t. A flow assigns to each edge an amount up to its capacity so that, at every vertex except s and t, inflow equals outflow.

nodes.title: String Algorithms
nodes.essence: Strings (sequences over an alphabet) are how computers hold text, source code, genomes, network payloads and logs. This area answers two questions. Where does a pattern occur in a text?

nodes.title: String Matching
nodes.essence: String matching finds every position where a pattern P of length m occurs in a text T of length n. The naive method tries each alignment and compares character by character, costing O(nm) in the worst case.

nodes.title: Tries and Suffix Structures
nodes.essence: A trie (prefix tree) stores a set of strings by sharing common prefixes: each edge is labelled by a character, and each key is a root-to-node path.

nodes.title: Advanced Topics
nodes.essence: The classical algorithms in this layer assume three things: the answer must be exact, the whole input is available up front, and memory is flat with unit-cost access. Real problems violate all three.

nodes.title: Approximation Algorithms
nodes.essence: For NP-hard optimisation problems (vertex cover, set cover, travelling salesperson, bin packing, scheduling) we do not expect an algorithm that is both exact and polynomial-time.

nodes.title: Streaming and Online Algorithms
nodes.essence: Classical algorithms see their whole input before deciding anything. Two important settings forbid this.

nodes.title: External Memory and Cache-Oblivious Algorithms
nodes.essence: The Random Access Machine (RAM) model charges one unit for any memory access, but real memory is a hierarchy in which each level is larger and slower than the one above and moves data in blocks: ~1 ns for a Level 1 (L1) cache hit, ~100 ns for Dynamic Random-Access Memory (DRAM), ~10–100 µs for a Solid-State Drive (SSD) read, ~5–10 ms for a disk seek (circa 2020s hardware).

nodes.title: Computational Geometry
nodes.essence: Computational geometry designs algorithms for points, segments, polygons and higher-dimensional shapes: convex hulls, line-segment intersections, nearest neighbours, triangulations, range searches and point location.

nodes.title: Programming Languages
nodes.essence: A programming language is a precisely defined notation for computation that humans can read, write and reason in, and that a machine can still execute.

nodes.title: Paradigms
nodes.essence: A paradigm is a model of what a program is. In the imperative view a program is a sequence of commands that change state. In the object-oriented view it is a collection of objects that hold state and respond to messages.

nodes.title: Imperative and Procedural Programming
nodes.essence: Imperative programming describes computation as a sequence of commands that change a program's state: variables are named memory cells, assignment overwrites them, and control flow (sequence, branch, loop) decides which command runs next.

nodes.title: Object-Oriented Programming
nodes.essence: Object-oriented programming (OOP) organises a program as a set of objects, each bundling some private state with the operations allowed to read or change it.

nodes.title: Functional Programming
nodes.essence: Functional programming treats a program as an expression to be evaluated rather than a list of commands to execute. Functions are values: they can be passed as arguments, returned as results and stored in data structures.

nodes.title: Logic and Declarative Programming
nodes.essence: Declarative programming states what result is wanted and leaves how to compute it to an engine.

nodes.title: Semantics and Types
nodes.essence: This area answers two questions: what does a program mean, and which programs should we refuse to run?

nodes.title: Syntax and Semantics
nodes.essence: Syntax is the form of a program: which strings of characters are legal and how they group into a tree. Semantics is the meaning: what a legal program computes. They are deliberately separate.

nodes.title: Binding, Scope and Closures
nodes.essence: A binding connects a name to the thing it denotes: a value, a memory location, a function or a type. Scope is the region of program text where a binding is visible; lifetime (extent) is the period of execution during which the bound entity exists.

nodes.title: Type Systems
nodes.essence: A type system is a set of rules that assigns a type to each expression in a program and rejects programs whose parts do not fit together.

nodes.title: Polymorphism and Type Inference
nodes.essence: Polymorphism lets one piece of code work for values of many types. Without it, a static type system would force you to write reverseIntList, reverseStringList and so on, separately, for every element type.

nodes.title: Compilers
nodes.essence: A compiler translates a program from a source language into a target language, usually machine code for an Instruction Set Architecture (ISA), while preserving its meaning. It is the bridge from the human-oriented abstractions of layer 06 back down to the hardware of layer 04.

nodes.title: Lexing and Parsing
nodes.essence: Lexing and parsing turn a flat string of characters into a tree that shows the program's structure. The lexer (scanner) groups characters into tokens such as identifiers, numbers, operators and keywords, discarding whitespace and comments.

nodes.title: Semantic Analysis
nodes.essence: Semantic analysis is the compiler phase that checks the rules a grammar cannot express and records what every name and expression means.

nodes.title: Intermediate Representations
nodes.essence: An Intermediate Representation (IR) is the compiler's internal language: a form of the program that sits between source and machine code and is designed for analysis and transformation rather than for people.

nodes.title: Optimization
nodes.essence: Compiler optimisation rewrites a program into one that computes the same observable result using less time, memory or energy.

nodes.title: Code Generation and Register Allocation
nodes.essence: Code generation is the compiler's back end: it maps the machine-independent Intermediate Representation (IR) onto the concrete instructions, registers and calling conventions of one Instruction Set Architecture (ISA). It solves three linked problems.

nodes.title: Runtime Systems
nodes.essence: A compiler finishes its work before the program starts; a runtime system is everything a language implementation still needs while the program runs.

nodes.title: Linking and Loading
nodes.essence: Large programs are compiled one file at a time, so each object file refers to functions and variables it does not define and does not know the final addresses of its own code.

nodes.title: Interpreters and Virtual Machines
nodes.essence: An interpreter executes a program directly, reading its representation and performing each operation, instead of translating the whole program to machine code first.

nodes.title: JIT Compilation
nodes.essence: Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation translates code to native machine instructions while the program is running, instead of before it starts. It exists to resolve a tension: portable, dynamic languages are naturally interpreted, and interpretation is slow.

nodes.title: Memory Management and Garbage Collection
nodes.essence: Programs create data whose lifetime does not follow the call stack: objects shared between parts of a program, closures that outlive their scope, nodes in a growing graph. Such data lives on the heap, and something must decide when each heap object can be freed.

nodes.title: Formal Methods
nodes.essence: Testing shows that a program works on the inputs you tried; formal methods show that it works on all of them.

nodes.title: Hoare Logic and Program Proofs
nodes.essence: Hoare logic (Hoare, 1969, building on Floyd, 1967) is a formal system for proving that imperative programs meet their specifications.

nodes.title: Model Checking
nodes.essence: Model checking (Clarke and Emerson, 1981; Queille and Sifakis, 1982) verifies a system automatically by exploring every state it can reach and checking that a property holds in all of them.

nodes.title: Proof Assistants and Dependent Types
nodes.essence: A proof assistant (interactive theorem prover) is a program in which a human writes definitions, specifications and proofs, and the machine checks every step. The user states a goal and applies tactics that break it into subgoals; the system refuses any unjustified step.

nodes.title: Operating Systems
nodes.essence: An Operating System (OS) is the program that turns one bare machine into a safe, shared, convenient one. Bare hardware offers a handful of cores, a flat physical memory, some disks and some devices, all reachable by any instruction that happens to run.

nodes.title: Kernel and Abstractions
nodes.essence: This area answers two questions: what is an Operating System (OS) for, and how does a piece of software get the authority to do it? The answer to the first is that the OS turns raw, shared, dangerous hardware into safe, private, convenient abstractions.

nodes.title: The Role of the OS
nodes.essence: An Operating System (OS) is the software that sits between hardware and programs and does three jobs: it virtualizes the hardware (one Central Processing Unit (CPU) becomes many processes, one physical memory becomes many private address spaces), it mediates concurrency among everything that shares the machine, and it provides persistence (named files that survive power loss).

nodes.title: Kernel Mode and System Calls
nodes.essence: The Central Processing Unit (CPU) has at least two privilege modes. In kernel mode it may execute every instruction and touch every address; in user mode privileged instructions fault and memory is limited to what the page tables allow.

nodes.title: Kernel Architectures
nodes.essence: A kernel architecture answers one question: which Operating System (OS) services run in privileged kernel mode, and which run as ordinary protected processes?

nodes.title: Process Management
nodes.essence: This area is how the Operating System (OS) virtualizes the Central Processing Unit (CPU). A machine has a few cores; users want hundreds of programs running at once, each written as if it had a processor to itself.

nodes.title: Processes
nodes.essence: A process is a program in execution: an isolated address space holding code, data, heap and stack, plus one or more threads of control, plus kernel-held resources such as open files, credentials and signal handlers.

nodes.title: Threads
nodes.essence: A thread is a single sequential flow of control: a program counter, a register set and a stack. A process may contain many threads that share its address space, heap, global variables and open files, while each has its own stack and registers.

nodes.title: Scheduling
nodes.essence: A scheduler decides which runnable thread runs on each Central Processing Unit (CPU) core and for how long.

nodes.title: Inter-Process Communication
nodes.essence: Inter-Process Communication (IPC) is the set of kernel-mediated channels that open a controlled hole in the isolation between processes. There are two families.

nodes.title: Concurrency
nodes.essence: When several threads share memory, the result of a program can depend on the order in which their instructions interleave, and that order is chosen by the scheduler and the hardware, not by the programmer.

nodes.title: Race Conditions and Critical Sections
nodes.essence: A race condition is a bug where a program's result depends on the timing of operations in concurrent threads. It arises when two or more threads access the same data, at least one writes, and nothing forces an order between them.

nodes.title: Locks and Semaphores
nodes.essence: A lock (mutex) is an object with two operations, acquire and release, that guarantees at most one thread holds it at a time; wrapping a critical section in acquire/release makes it mutually exclusive.

nodes.title: Condition Variables and Monitors
nodes.essence: Locks stop threads from interfering, but threads also need to wait for something to become true: a queue to become non-empty, a child to finish, a buffer to have space. Spinning on a flag wastes the Central Processing Unit (CPU) and races with the writer.

nodes.title: Deadlock
nodes.essence: A deadlock is a state in which a set of threads each waits for a resource held by another thread in the set, so none can ever proceed. The classic case is two threads and two locks: T1 holds A and wants B, T2 holds B and wants A.

nodes.title: Lock-Free Synchronization
nodes.essence: Lock-free (more generally, non-blocking) synchronization lets threads share data structures without mutual exclusion.

nodes.title: Memory Management
nodes.essence: This area is how the Operating System (OS) virtualizes memory. Physical memory is one shared array of bytes of fixed size; each program wants a large, private, contiguous address space that starts at the same place every time and is protected from every other program.

nodes.title: Address Spaces and Paging
nodes.essence: An address space is the range of virtual addresses a process can use, together with what each address maps to.

nodes.title: Page Replacement
nodes.essence: When physical memory is full and a process touches a page that is not resident, the Operating System (OS) must choose a victim page to evict, writing it to disk first if it has been modified.

nodes.title: Memory Allocation
nodes.essence: Memory allocation hands out pieces of memory on request and takes them back. It happens at two levels. The kernel allocates physical frames (for page tables, page cache and user pages) and small kernel objects (process records, inodes, socket buffers).

nodes.title: Storage and File Systems
nodes.essence: This area is the Operating System's (OS's) third job: persistence. Memory forgets everything when power fails; storage devices remember, but only as a flat array of fixed-size blocks with no names, no structure, no protection and no guarantee about which writes survive a crash.

nodes.title: File System Abstractions
nodes.essence: A file system gives programs two abstractions over raw storage. A file is a named, persistent, growable array of bytes, with no structure imposed by the Operating System (OS).

nodes.title: File System Implementation
nodes.essence: A file system implementation is a data structure laid out on a block device.

nodes.title: Crash Consistency and Journaling
nodes.essence: Most file system operations change several blocks: appending to a file updates a data block, the inode (size, block map) and the free-space bitmap.

nodes.title: I/O and Devices
nodes.essence: Computers exist to take in and emit data, yet devices are wildly diverse (keyboards, disks, network cards, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs)) and wildly slower or faster than the Central Processing Unit (CPU) expects. This area answers two questions.

nodes.title: Device Drivers and Interrupt Handling
nodes.essence: A device driver is kernel code that knows how to operate one kind of device: which registers to write to start an operation, how to set up Direct Memory Access (DMA) so the device moves data to or from memory itself, and how to interpret the device's status.

nodes.title: I/O Models
nodes.essence: An input/output (I/O) model is the contract for how a program waits for I/O. In blocking I/O, read puts the thread to sleep until data arrives: simple, but each in-flight operation needs a thread.

nodes.title: Virtualization
nodes.essence: The Operating System (OS) virtualizes the Central Processing Unit (CPU) and memory for processes. This area applies the same trick one level further, to isolate whole software environments from each other on shared hardware. Two designs dominate.

nodes.title: Virtual Machines and Hypervisors
nodes.essence: A hypervisor (virtual machine monitor, VMM) runs several virtual machines (VMs), each a faithful copy of the real hardware on which an unmodified Operating System (OS) can run.

nodes.title: Containers
nodes.essence: A container is a group of ordinary processes that the kernel shows a private view of the system: their own process identifiers (IDs), mount tree, network interfaces, hostname and users, with limits on how much Central Processing Unit (CPU), memory and input/output (I/O) they may consume.

nodes.title: Networking
nodes.essence: Networking answers one question: how do programs on different machines exchange data reliably and efficiently when the only thing connecting them is a shared, lossy, delay-prone physical medium owned by many parties?

nodes.title: Principles
nodes.essence: Before any specific protocol, three ideas decide the shape of every network built since the 1970s. First, where should a function live: in the network or at its edges?

nodes.title: Layering and the End-to-End Principle
nodes.essence: A network protocol stack splits the job of moving data into layers, each offering a service to the layer above using only the service of the layer below. Each layer wraps the data from above in its own header (encapsulation) and its peer on the far side strips it off.

nodes.title: Packet Switching
nodes.essence: Packet switching breaks data into self-contained packets, each carrying its destination address, and lets every link be shared on demand by whoever has packets to send.

nodes.title: Latency, Bandwidth and Queueing
nodes.essence: Two numbers describe a network path: latency, how long one bit takes to get from sender to receiver, and bandwidth, how many bits per second the path can carry. They are independent: a truck full of disks has huge bandwidth and terrible latency.

nodes.title: Link Layer
nodes.essence: The link layer moves a frame of bits from one device to a directly connected neighbour: across a cable, through a switch, or over a radio channel.

nodes.title: Encoding and Framing
nodes.essence: A link is a physical channel that carries a continuous signal.

nodes.title: Media Access and Ethernet
nodes.essence: When several stations share one transmission medium, two frames sent at once collide and both are lost. A Medium Access Control (MAC) protocol decides who may send when, with no central coordinator and no prior knowledge of who has data.

nodes.title: Wireless Networks
nodes.essence: Radio is a shared broadcast medium whose quality changes from moment to moment. Signal strength falls steeply with distance, reflects off walls, and fades as people move.

nodes.title: Network Layer
nodes.essence: The network layer delivers a packet from any host to any other host across many independent links and networks. It answers two separate questions. Forwarding: when a packet arrives at a router, which output port should it leave by?

nodes.title: IP Addressing and Forwarding
nodes.essence: The Internet Protocol (IP) gives every network interface an address and defines a packet format that any network can carry. Addresses are hierarchical: a prefix names a network, the remaining bits name a host within it.

nodes.title: Routing Algorithms
nodes.essence: A routing algorithm fills every router's forwarding table so that hop-by-hop decisions deliver packets along good paths. The network is a graph: routers are nodes, links are edges weighted by a cost such as delay or inverse bandwidth.

nodes.title: Internet Routing and BGP
nodes.essence: The Internet is not one network but about 75,000 independently operated networks called Autonomous Systems (ASes), circa mid-2020s. Inside each, operators run whatever routing they like.

nodes.title: Data Center Networks and SDN
nodes.essence: A large data center holds tens to hundreds of thousands of servers owned by one operator, and its network is a different problem from the Internet.

nodes.title: Transport Layer
nodes.essence: The network layer delivers packets between hosts, unreliably.

nodes.title: UDP and TCP
nodes.essence: The Internet offers two classic transport services on top of the Internet Protocol (IP). The User Datagram Protocol (UDP) adds only port numbers and a checksum: each message is an independent datagram that may be lost, duplicated or reordered.

nodes.title: Reliable Delivery
nodes.essence: Reliable delivery turns a channel that can lose, corrupt, duplicate and reorder packets into one that delivers every byte exactly once and in order.

nodes.title: Congestion Control
nodes.essence: When senders inject packets faster than a bottleneck link can drain them, queues grow, delay rises and packets are dropped; senders retransmit, adding more load, and useful throughput can collapse.

nodes.title: Application Layer
nodes.essence: The transport layer gives two processes a byte stream. The application layer decides what those bytes mean: how a user names what they want, how a request is phrased, how a response is cached and reused.

nodes.title: Naming and DNS
nodes.essence: People and programs want stable, meaningful names such as www.example.com; networks route by numeric addresses that change when services move. The Domain Name System (DNS) is a globally distributed database that maps names to addresses and other records.

nodes.title: HTTP and the Web
nodes.essence: The web is three inventions combined by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989–91: a way to name any resource anywhere (the Uniform Resource Locator, URL), a document format that links to other resources by name (the HyperText Markup Language, HTML), and a protocol to fetch a named resource (the Hypertext Transfer Protocol, HTTP).

nodes.title: Content Delivery and Caching
nodes.essence: Most Internet traffic is a small set of popular objects (videos, images, scripts, software updates) read by many people far from where they were published.

nodes.title: Data Management
nodes.essence: Data management is the discipline of durable, shared, queryable state. Durable: data survives crashes and power loss. Shared: many users and programs read and change it at once without corrupting it.

nodes.title: Data Models
nodes.essence: A data model is the vocabulary a database offers for describing and querying data: what shapes data can take, what constraints it must obey, and what operations exist. It is the logical interface between applications and storage.

nodes.title: The Relational Model
nodes.essence: The relational model represents all data as relations: named sets of tuples, where each tuple assigns a value to each of a fixed set of named attributes. Relationships between entities are expressed by matching values (keys), not by pointers.

nodes.title: Relational Algebra and SQL
nodes.essence: Relational algebra is a small set of operators that each take one or two relations and return a relation: select rows, project columns, take products, union, difference and rename.

nodes.title: Normalization
nodes.essence: Normalization is the theory of designing relational schemas so that each fact is stored exactly once.

nodes.title: Non-Relational Models
nodes.essence: Non-relational data models (often grouped under the label "NoSQL") give up some part of the relational design (fixed schema, joins, general transactions or declarative queries) in exchange for a better fit to a particular access pattern or easier horizontal scaling.

nodes.title: Storage and Indexing
nodes.essence: Storage and indexing answer the physical question: given relations defined logically, how should their bytes be arranged on devices so that the queries and updates that matter are cheap? The governing fact is the memory hierarchy.

nodes.title: Storage Layouts
nodes.essence: A database stores relations as records packed into fixed-size pages (typically 4–16 KB), and pages into files or raw device regions. Pages are the unit of transfer between storage and memory, and a buffer pool in memory caches the pages in use.

nodes.title: B-Trees
nodes.essence: A B-tree is a balanced search tree whose nodes are disk pages, each holding hundreds of keys and child pointers.

nodes.title: LSM-Trees
nodes.essence: A Log-Structured Merge-tree (LSM-tree) makes writes cheap by never updating data in place. New writes go to a sorted in-memory buffer (the memtable) and to a sequential log for durability.

nodes.title: Query Processing
nodes.essence: A declarative query says what result is wanted. Query processing turns it into a program that computes that result efficiently over the actual storage.

nodes.title: Join Algorithms
nodes.essence: A join combines two relations by matching tuples on a condition, usually equality of keys. Defined as a Cartesian product followed by a selection, a join of two million-row tables would examine 10^12 pairs.

nodes.title: Query Optimization
nodes.essence: A query optimizer takes a declarative query and chooses, among the many equivalent ways to execute it, one that is cheap. It works in three parts. A plan space: all algebra trees equivalent to the query, crossed with choices of access path and join algorithm for each node.

nodes.title: Transactions
nodes.essence: Many users change a shared database at once, and the machine can crash at any moment. Without help, every application would have to reason about every possible interleaving with every other program and every possible point of failure.

nodes.title: ACID
nodes.essence: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability (ACID) names the four guarantees of a database transaction: Atomicity (all of its effects happen or none do), Consistency (it moves the database from one state satisfying the integrity constraints to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's partial work; the result is as if they ran one at a time) and Durability (once committed, its effects survive crashes).

nodes.title: Concurrency Control
nodes.essence: Concurrency control lets many transactions run at once while guaranteeing the result is equivalent to running them one at a time in some order (serializability).

nodes.title: Isolation Levels
nodes.essence: Full serializability costs concurrency, so databases offer weaker isolation levels that permit specific anomalies in exchange for throughput.

nodes.title: Recovery and Logging
nodes.essence: Recovery provides atomicity and durability when the system crashes and loses everything in memory.

nodes.title: Distributed and Parallel Computing
nodes.essence: This layer asks how many computers, or many processors in one computer, can do one job together. Parallel computing uses many processors to finish a job faster.

nodes.title: Parallel Computing
nodes.essence: Parallel computing asks how to finish one computation faster by running parts of it at the same time on many processing units.

nodes.title: Work, Span and Parallel Models
nodes.essence: A parallel computation is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of operations, where an edge means "this must finish before that starts". Two numbers summarise the graph. Work (T1) is the total number of operations, the time on one processor.

nodes.title: Data and Task Parallelism
nodes.essence: There are two basic ways to find independent work. Data parallelism applies the same operation to many data items at once: the parallelism grows with the data. Task parallelism runs different operations at once: the parallelism is fixed by the structure of the program.

nodes.title: Parallel Programming Models
nodes.essence: A parallel programming model is the contract between the programmer and the parallel machine: how work is expressed, how data is shared or exchanged, and how workers synchronise. Two choices define most models.

nodes.title: Distributed Foundations
nodes.essence: A distributed system is a set of computers that cooperate only by sending messages over a network, where any computer or link can fail independently.

nodes.title: System Models and Failures
nodes.essence: A system model is the precise list of assumptions a distributed algorithm is allowed to make: how processes can fail, how messages can misbehave, and what is known about timing.

nodes.title: Time, Clocks and Ordering
nodes.essence: Machines in a distributed system have no shared clock. Each has a quartz oscillator that drifts, and synchronising them over a network with variable delay leaves an uncertainty of microseconds to milliseconds.

nodes.title: Impossibility Results
nodes.essence: A handful of theorems mark the boundaries of what distributed systems can do; their value lies in their exact assumptions. Two Generals: no protocol over a lossy channel guarantees that two parties agree to act together.

nodes.title: Consensus and Replication
nodes.essence: To survive the loss of a machine, a system keeps copies of its state on several machines. The moment there are copies, they can disagree: a write reaches one copy and not another, or two clients write different copies at once.

nodes.title: Replication
nodes.essence: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines, for three reasons: to survive machine loss (durability and availability), to serve more reads (throughput), and to put data near users (latency). Copying immutable data is easy; the whole difficulty is changes.

nodes.title: Consensus
nodes.essence: Consensus is the problem of getting a group of processes to agree on one value even though some may crash and messages may be delayed.

nodes.title: Consistency Models
nodes.essence: A consistency model is a contract between a replicated store and its clients: it says which values a read may return, given the writes that happened.

nodes.title: Byzantine Fault Tolerance
nodes.essence: Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) is consensus and replication when faulty nodes may behave arbitrarily: send conflicting messages to different peers, forge claims, stay silent selectively, or collude. The name comes from Lamport, Shostak and Pease's "Byzantine Generals" (1982).

nodes.title: Distributed Data
nodes.essence: When a dataset or its write load outgrows one machine, it must be split across many.

nodes.title: Partitioning
nodes.essence: Partitioning (also called sharding) splits a dataset into disjoint pieces stored on different nodes, so that storage and write throughput grow with the number of nodes.

nodes.title: Distributed Transactions
nodes.essence: A distributed transaction reads and writes data on several nodes and must still be atomic (all nodes commit or all abort) and isolated (concurrent transactions appear to run one at a time).

nodes.title: Eventual Consistency and CRDTs
nodes.essence: Eventual consistency lets every replica accept reads and writes locally, without waiting for others, and promises only that replicas converge once they have received the same updates.

nodes.title: Large-Scale Systems
nodes.essence: This area is about whole systems that run on thousands of machines and serve millions of users or process petabytes of data: data pipelines, cloud platforms and internet services.

nodes.title: Batch and Stream Processing
nodes.essence: Batch processing runs a computation over a large, finite dataset and produces an output; stream processing runs a computation continuously over an unbounded sequence of events and updates its output as events arrive.

nodes.title: Cloud Computing
nodes.essence: Cloud computing turns data centres into pooled resources (compute, storage, networking and higher-level services) that customers rent on demand through an Application Programming Interface (API) and pay for by use.

nodes.title: Scalability Patterns
nodes.essence: A system scales if adding resources adds proportional capacity without a redesign.

nodes.title: Security and Cryptography
nodes.essence: Security is the study of how systems keep working as intended when someone is actively trying to make them fail. Every other layer in this tree designs against nature: noise, wear, random failures, honest mistakes.

nodes.title: Security Principles
nodes.essence: Before choosing a cipher or a firewall rule, you must say what you are protecting, from whom, and what you are willing to trust. This area supplies that vocabulary and the design rules that have proved durable since the 1970s.

nodes.title: CIA and Threat Modeling
nodes.essence: Security goals are usually stated as the CIA triad, named for its three goals: confidentiality (information is disclosed only to those authorised), integrity (information and systems are changed only in authorised ways, and changes are detectable), and availability (authorised users can use the system when they need it).

nodes.title: Security Design Principles
nodes.essence: Security design principles are rules for structuring a system so that it resists attack even when individual components have bugs.

nodes.title: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies
nodes.essence: Confidentiality asks who may read this data; privacy asks what may be learned about a person, even by parties allowed to see the data. Encryption and access control cannot answer that: the threat is often the authorised recipient, a published statistic or communication metadata.

nodes.title: Cryptography
nodes.essence: Cryptography is the science of protecting information from an adversary who can see, alter or inject data you do not physically control: data on a network, on a stolen laptop, in someone else's data centre.

nodes.title: Foundations of Modern Cryptography
nodes.essence: Modern cryptography, as developed from the late 1970s onward, rests on three steps. First, a precise definition of what it means to break a scheme, written as a game between a challenger and an adversary with stated powers.

nodes.title: Symmetric Encryption
nodes.essence: Symmetric encryption protects confidentiality when sender and receiver share a secret key. It is fast (gigabytes per second per core with hardware support) and does nearly all bulk encryption in practice; public-key methods are used mainly to agree on symmetric keys.

nodes.title: Hash Functions and MACs
nodes.essence: A cryptographic hash function maps input of any length to a short fixed-length digest (256 bits for SHA-256, a member of the Secure Hash Algorithm 2 (SHA-2) family) such that no one can feasibly find two inputs with the same digest, or an input matching a given digest.

nodes.title: Public-Key Cryptography
nodes.essence: Two strangers on the internet share no secret key. Public-key (asymmetric) cryptography solves this by giving each party a key pair: a public key anyone may know and a private key only its owner holds.

nodes.title: Secure Protocols and TLS
nodes.essence: A secure channel protocol combines primitives into a connection that gives confidentiality, integrity and authentication of at least one endpoint over a network the attacker controls.

nodes.title: System Security
nodes.essence: System security asks how a single computer, shared by many programs and users who do not fully trust each other, keeps each from reading or corrupting what belongs to the others.

nodes.title: Access Control
nodes.essence: Access control decides whether a subject (a user, process or service) may perform an operation on an object (a file, record, device or Application Programming Interface (API) endpoint).

nodes.title: Memory Safety Vulnerabilities
nodes.essence: In languages such as C and C++, the program is trusted to keep every memory access within the bounds and lifetime of the object it means to touch; the language and hardware do not check.

nodes.title: Isolation and Sandboxing
nodes.essence: Isolation confines a piece of code so that, even if it is buggy or malicious, it cannot read or modify anything outside an assigned set of resources.

nodes.title: Side Channels
nodes.essence: A side channel is information that leaks through the physical behaviour of a computation rather than through its intended outputs: how long it takes, which cache lines it touches, how much power it draws, what electromagnetic radiation or sound it emits.

nodes.title: Network and Application Security
nodes.essence: Most attacks arrive over a network and target an application: a login form, a web page, an exposed service, a routing protocol.

nodes.title: Authentication
nodes.essence: Authentication is establishing that a party is who it claims to be, so that access-control decisions and audit records can be tied to a real principal.

nodes.title: Web Security
nodes.essence: The web runs code from millions of mutually distrusting sources inside one program, the browser, which also holds the user's sessions for every site they use.

nodes.title: Network Attacks and Defenses
nodes.essence: The Internet's core protocols were designed for a cooperative network of research institutions. Source addresses are not verified, routing announcements are mostly believed, name lookups are not authenticated, and anyone can send traffic to anyone.

nodes.title: Software Supply Chain Security
nodes.essence: The program you run is not the source you reviewed. Between them stand third-party packages, their maintainers, a registry, a compiler, a build server, a signing key and an update channel, and any of them can insert code that runs with your program's privileges.

nodes.title: Software Engineering
nodes.essence: Programming is making a computer do something. Software engineering is keeping that working while the code, the people and the requirements all change.

nodes.title: Design
nodes.essence: Software design answers one question: how should a system be divided so that people can understand it and change it? Any working program has some structure, and many structures produce the same behaviour.

nodes.title: Essential and Accidental Complexity
nodes.essence: Fred Brooks split the difficulty of building software into two parts ("No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accident in Software Engineering", 1986). Essential complexity belongs to the problem: the business rules, the edge cases, the outside systems you must talk to.

nodes.title: Modularity and Information Hiding
nodes.essence: A module is a part of a system that can be designed, understood and changed with limited knowledge of the rest. Splitting a system into modules is easy; splitting it so that changes stay inside one module is the hard part.

nodes.title: Abstraction and Interfaces
nodes.essence: An abstraction is a simplified view of something that keeps what a user needs and omits the rest. An interface is the concrete form of that view: the operations, their types and the promises about their behaviour.

nodes.title: Design Patterns
nodes.essence: A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a problem that recurs in a context, described with its trade-offs.

nodes.title: Software Architecture
nodes.essence: Software architecture is the set of structural decisions about a whole system that are expensive to change: how it is divided into components, how they communicate, where state lives, and what is deployed together.

nodes.title: Process
nodes.essence: Design decides the shape of the code. Process decides how a group of people, over time, discovers what to build, builds it in steps, and keeps a coherent record of every change.

nodes.title: Requirements
nodes.essence: Requirements say what a system must do and how well, in terms of the world it serves rather than the code inside it.

nodes.title: Development Lifecycles
nodes.essence: A development lifecycle is the order in which a team specifies, designs, builds, tests and releases software, and how often it repeats. The core variable is the length of the feedback loop: how long between making a decision and learning whether it was right.

nodes.title: Version Control
nodes.essence: A version control system (VCS) records every change to a set of files, who made it, when and why, and lets many people change the same files in parallel and combine their work.

nodes.title: Conway's Law and Teams
nodes.essence: Melvin Conway observed in 1968 ("How Do Committees Invent?") that "organizations which design systems ... are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations." The mechanism is simple: two modules can only work together if the people building them agree on an interface, and people agree most easily with those they talk to often.

nodes.title: Quality
nodes.essence: Quality engineering asks: how do we gain justified confidence that software does what it should, and find out quickly when it does not?

nodes.title: Testing
nodes.essence: Testing runs a program on chosen inputs and checks the results against an oracle, some independent statement of what the right result is. It is the main way software teams gain confidence that code works and keeps working as it changes.

nodes.title: Debugging
nodes.essence: Debugging is finding the cause of an observed failure and removing it. The difficulty is that cause and symptom are separated in space and time: a wrong value written in one function may surface as a crash far away, much later.

nodes.title: Static Analysis and Code Review
nodes.essence: Static analysis and code review both examine code without running it. Static analysis does it by machine: type checkers, linters, data-flow analysers and verifiers reason about all possible executions of a program at once, for a narrow set of properties.

nodes.title: Operations
nodes.essence: Software delivers value only when it runs in front of users, and most modern software runs as a continuously operated service rather than a shipped product.

nodes.title: Build and Continuous Delivery
nodes.essence: A build turns source code into runnable artifacts; a delivery pipeline takes each change from commit to production. Continuous integration (CI) means every change is merged into the main line and automatically built and tested, many times a day.

nodes.title: Reliability Engineering
nodes.essence: Reliability engineering keeps a service working well enough for its users while it changes.

nodes.title: Observability
nodes.essence: Observability is the ability to understand what a running system is doing, and why, from the data it emits. The term comes from control theory (Kalman, 1960), where a system is observable if its internal state can be inferred from its outputs.

nodes.title: Artificial Intelligence
nodes.essence: Artificial Intelligence (AI) asks how to build programs that act sensibly in situations their programmers did not spell out case by case: recognise a face, plan a route, play a game, answer a question, write code.

nodes.title: Classical AI
nodes.essence: Classical Artificial Intelligence (AI), dominant from the 1956 Dartmouth workshop to the 1990s, asks: if a human writes down what the world is like and what the goal is, can a general algorithm work out what to do?

nodes.title: Search and Planning
nodes.essence: Many problems an intelligent agent faces can be stated as: here is where I am, here is what I want, here are the moves I can make; find a sequence of moves.

nodes.title: Constraint Satisfaction
nodes.essence: A Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) asks for values for a set of variables such that every constraint among them holds: colour a map so neighbours differ, schedule exams so no student has two at once, fill a Sudoku.

nodes.title: Knowledge Representation and Reasoning
nodes.essence: Knowledge Representation and Reasoning (KR&R) asks how to write down what an agent knows so that a machine can derive what follows from it.

nodes.title: Probabilistic Reasoning
nodes.essence: Real agents never know the world exactly: sensors are noisy, rules have exceptions, and the future is uncertain. Probabilistic reasoning represents belief as a probability distribution and updates it with Bayes' rule as evidence arrives.

nodes.title: Machine Learning Foundations
nodes.essence: Machine Learning (ML) answers the question: how can a program acquire behaviour from examples instead of from a programmer? Its answer has three parts that every child of this node elaborates. Choose a family of functions with adjustable parameters.

nodes.title: Learning as Optimization
nodes.essence: Machine Learning (ML) replaces hand-written rules with a parameterised function f_θ and a procedure that adjusts the parameters θ so that the function behaves well on examples.

nodes.title: Generalization and Bias-Variance
nodes.essence: A model is useful only if it performs well on data it has not seen. Generalisation is the gap between training performance and performance on new data drawn from the same distribution.

nodes.title: Supervised Learning
nodes.essence: Supervised learning learns a function from input to output using examples where the right answer is given: emails labelled spam or not, images labelled with objects, houses with sale prices. If the output is a category it is classification; if it is a number it is regression.

nodes.title: Unsupervised Learning
nodes.essence: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data without labels: groups of similar items, a few directions that explain most variation, or the probability distribution the data came from.

nodes.title: Evaluation and Experimentation
nodes.essence: A learned model has no specification to verify against; its behaviour is defined by data.

nodes.title: Deep Learning
nodes.essence: Deep learning is Machine Learning (ML) with deep neural networks: long compositions of simple differentiable layers trained end to end by gradient descent.

nodes.title: Neural Networks and Backpropagation
nodes.essence: A neural network is a function built by composing many simple layers, each a linear map followed by a fixed non-linearity: h = σ(Wx + b).
