nodes.title: Convolutional Networks
nodes.essence: A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is a neural network built for data on a grid, such as images, audio spectrograms or video.

nodes.title: Recurrent Networks and Sequence Models
nodes.essence: Text, speech and sensor streams arrive as sequences of varying length, and each element's meaning depends on what came before.

nodes.title: Attention and Transformers
nodes.essence: Attention lets every element of a sequence look at every other element and pull in information from the ones that matter, with "what matters" computed from the content itself.

nodes.title: Training at Scale
nodes.essence: The largest neural networks as of the mid-2020s have hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters and are trained on tens of trillions of tokens, needing on the order of 10^24 to 10^26 floating-point operations.

nodes.title: Advanced Paradigms
nodes.essence: The foundations of Machine Learning (ML) assume a fixed dataset of inputs and labels and a model that predicts. This area covers what happens when those assumptions are dropped. Reinforcement learning (RL) drops the labels: an agent learns from rewards earned by acting.

nodes.title: Reinforcement Learning
nodes.essence: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is learning to act from trial and error. An agent observes a state, takes an action, receives a numerical reward and a new state, and must learn a policy that maximises total reward over time.

nodes.title: Generative Models
nodes.essence: A generative model learns the probability distribution p(x) that a dataset was drawn from, so that it can produce new samples that look like the data: images, audio, text, molecules.

nodes.title: Large Language Models
nodes.essence: A Large Language Model (LLM) is a transformer, typically with billions to trillions of parameters, trained to predict the next token of text over a corpus of trillions of tokens.

nodes.title: Retrieval and Embeddings
nodes.essence: An embedding is a learned map from an object (a word, passage, image or user) to a vector, trained so that closeness means similarity for some task.

nodes.title: Alignment and Safety
nodes.essence: Alignment is the problem of getting a learned system to pursue the goals its designers and users actually intend, rather than a proxy that diverges from them; safety is the broader discipline of keeping Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems from causing harm through error, misuse or unintended behaviour.

nodes.title: Human and Visual Computing
nodes.essence: Every computation that matters to a person eventually passes through human senses: light from a screen, sound from a speaker, a touch or a keystroke going back in. This layer covers the boundary where computation meets human perception.

nodes.title: Human-Computer Interaction
nodes.essence: Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) studies the boundary where a person and a computer exchange intent and information. The question it answers is: how do we build systems that people can actually use to reach their goals, quickly, correctly and without frustration?

nodes.title: Perception and Cognition
nodes.essence: Every interactive system ends at a human, and the human is a fixed piece of hardware with known limits.

nodes.title: Interaction Design Principles
nodes.essence: Interaction design decides how people tell a computer what they want and how the computer shows what it did. A user starts with a goal, must translate it into actions the system accepts, and must interpret the system's response to judge whether the goal was met.

nodes.title: Usability Evaluation
nodes.essence: Designers cannot judge the usability of their own work: they know how it is supposed to work, so they cannot see it as a newcomer does. Usability evaluation replaces opinion with evidence by observing or measuring real users doing real tasks.

nodes.title: Information Visualization
nodes.essence: Information visualization turns data into pictures so that people can use their visual system, the brain's highest-bandwidth input, to see patterns, outliers and comparisons invisible in a table.

nodes.title: Computer Graphics
nodes.essence: Computer graphics answers the question: given a mathematical description of a scene (shapes, materials, lights, a camera), what image would a viewer see? It is the forward problem of vision.

nodes.title: Geometry and Transformations
nodes.essence: Computer graphics turns a mathematical description of a 3D scene into a 2D image.

nodes.title: Rasterization Pipeline
nodes.essence: Rasterisation draws a 3D scene by projecting each triangle onto the screen and filling in the pixels it covers. It answers the visibility question object by object: for each triangle, which pixels does it touch, and is it nearer than whatever is already drawn there?

nodes.title: Ray Tracing and Global Illumination
nodes.essence: Ray tracing renders an image by following light backwards: from the camera through each pixel into the scene, finding the first surface hit, then asking where the light arriving at that point came from.

nodes.title: Media and Vision
nodes.essence: This area deals with images, audio and video as data: how to capture and store them efficiently, and how to make machines understand them. Its two children face opposite directions.

nodes.title: Digital Media and Compression
nodes.essence: Images, audio and video are continuous signals that must be sampled and quantised to become bits, and the raw result is enormous: one second of uncompressed 4K video at 60 frames per second is about 1.5 GB (gigabytes).

nodes.title: Computer Vision
nodes.essence: Computer vision extracts meaning and structure from images and video: what objects are present, where they are, how the camera moved, what 3D shape produced the picture. It is the inverse of graphics.

nodes.title: Computing in Context
nodes.essence: Every layer below this one asks how to make computation correct, fast, reliable or useful. This layer asks what computation does to the people and societies that build and use it, and what they in turn do to it.

nodes.title: History of Computing
nodes.essence: The history of computing is the story of two roots, one formal and one physical, joining and then being scaled up by many orders of magnitude.

nodes.title: Ethics and Professional Responsibility
nodes.essence: Computing professionals build systems that act on people who never agreed to the design and often cannot see it. Ethics is the discipline of asking, before and during building, who is affected, how they could be harmed, and what the builder owes them.

nodes.title: Law, Privacy and Policy
nodes.essence: Law and policy turn some expectations about technology into enforceable rules. For computing the main areas are privacy and data protection, intellectual property, liability and safety, computer crime, competition, and speech on platforms.

nodes.title: Environmental Impact
nodes.essence: Every computation turns electricity into heat, and every device is made from mined and refined materials that eventually become waste.
